entries.dae7df223015f5733c1d920d16f335e272a1f295: <div sID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="2Kgs.23" sID="2Kgs.23"/> <div eID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7563" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7564" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The happy continuance of the goodness of Josiah's reign, and the progress of the reformation he began, reading the law (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.1-2Kgs.23.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), renewing the covenant (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.3">ver. 3</reference>), cleansing the temple (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">ver. 4</reference>), and rooting out idols and idolatry, with all the relics thereof, in all places, as far as his power reached (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5-2Kgs.23.20">ver. 5-20</reference>), keeping a solemn passover (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.21-2Kgs.23.23">ver. 21-23</reference>), and clearing the country of witches (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.24">ver. 24</reference>); and in all this acting with extraordinary vigour, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.25">ver. 25</reference> II. The unhappy conclusion of it in his untimely death, as a token of the continuance of God's wrath against Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26-2Kgs.23.30">ver. 26-30</reference> III. The more unhappy consequences of his death, in the bad reigns of his two sons Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim, that came after him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31-2Kgs.23.37">ver. 31-37</reference>
entries.8feef6d0aeeb71b48b93a4ba4bdae75af89e6591: <div eID="gen7564" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7563" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Josiah Destroys Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 623.)</title> <div sID="gen7565" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the king sent, and they gathered unto him all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the king went up into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the people, both small and great: and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to walk after the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all <hi type="italic">their</hi> heart and all <hi type="italic">their</hi> soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant. <div eID="gen7565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> Josiah had received a message from God that there was no preventing the ruin of Jerusalem, but that he should deliver only his own soul; yet he did not therefore sit down in despair, and resolve to do nothing for his country because he could not do all he would. No, he would do his duty, and then leave the event to God. A public reformation was the thing resolved on; if any thing could prevent the threatened ruin it must be that; and here we have the preparations for that reformation. 1. He summoned a general assembly of the states, the elders, the magistrates or representatives of Judah and Jerusalem, to meet him <hi type="italic">in the house of the Lord,</hi> with the priests and prophets, the ordinary and extraordinary ministers, that, they all joining in it, it might become a national act and so be the more likely to prevent national judgments; they were all called to attend (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.1-2Kgs.23.2">v. 1, 2</reference>), that the business might be done with the more solemnity, that they might all advise and assist in it, and that those who were against it might be discouraged from making any opposition. Parliaments are no diminution at all to the honour and power of good princes, but a great support to them. 2. Instead of making a speech to this convention, he ordered the book of the law to be read to them; nay, it should seem, he read it himself (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.2">v. 2</reference>), as one much affected with it and desirous that they should be so too. Josiah thinks it not below him to be a reader, any more than Solomon did to be a preacher, nay, and David himself to be a door-keeper in the house of God. Besides the convention of the great men, he had a congregation of the <hi type="italic">men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem</hi> to hear the law read. It is really the interest of princes to promote the knowledge of the scriptures in their dominions. If the people be but as stedfastly resolved to obey by law as he is to govern by law, the kingdom will be happy. All people are concerned to know the scripture, and all in authority to spread the knowledge of it. 3. Instead of proposing laws for the confirming of them in their duty, he proposed an association by which they should all jointly engage themselves to God, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.3">v. 3</reference>. The book of the law was the book of the covenant, that, if they would be to God a people, he would be to them a God; they here engage themselves to do their part, not doubting but that then God would do his. (1.) The covenant was that they should walk after the Lord, in compliance with his will, in his ordinances and his providences, should answer all his calls and attend all his motions—that they should make conscience of all his commandments, moral, ceremonial, and judicial, and should carefully observe them <hi type="italic">with all their heart and all their soul,</hi> with all possible care and caution, sincerity, vigour, courage, and resolution, and so fulfil the conditions of this covenant, in dependence upon the promises of it. (2.) The covenanters were, in the first place, the king himself, who stood by his pillar (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.14">ch. xi. 14</reference>) and publicly declared his consent to this covenant, to set them an example, and to assure them not only of his protection but of his presidency and all the furtherance his power could give them in their obedience. It is no abridgment of the liberty even of princes themselves to be in bonds to God. <hi type="italic">All the people</hi> likewise <hi type="italic">stood to the covenant,</hi> that is, they signified their consent to it and promised to abide by it. It is of good use to oblige ourselves to our duty with all possible solemnity, and this is especially seasonable after notorious backslidings to sin and decays in that which is good. He that bears an honest mind does not shrink from positive engagements: fast bind, fast find.
entries.9c00887ba4eef3cbb138b28a2231901a1da30122: <div eID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Josiah Reforms Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 623.)</title> <div sID="gen7567" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the door, to bring forth out of the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all the vessels that were made for Baal, and for the grove, and for all the host of heaven: and he burned them without Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, and carried the ashes of them unto Beth-el. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he put down the idolatrous priests, whom the kings of Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places in the cities of Judah, and in the places round about Jerusalem; them also that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, and to the planets, and to all the host of heaven. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he brought out the grove from the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , without Jerusalem, unto the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and stamped <hi type="italic">it</hi> small to powder, and cast the powder thereof upon the graves of the children of the people. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he brake down the houses of the sodomites, that <hi type="italic">were</hi> by the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , where the women wove hangings for the grove. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where the priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beer-sheba, and brake down the high places of the gates that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the entering in of the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> on a man's left hand at the gate of the city. <hi type="super">9</hi> Nevertheless the priests of the high places came not up to the altar of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in Jerusalem, but they did eat of the unleavened bread among their brethren. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he defiled Topheth, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun, at the entering in of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , by the chamber of Nathan-melech the chamberlain, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the suburbs, and burned the chariots of the sun with fire. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the altars that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars which Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , did the king beat down, and brake <hi type="italic">them</hi> down from thence, and cast the dust of them into the brook Kidron. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the high places that <hi type="italic">were</hi> before Jerusalem, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he brake in pieces the images, and cut down the groves, and filled their places with the bones of men. <hi type="super">15</hi> Moreover the altar that <hi type="italic">was</hi> at Beth-el, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the high place which Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, had made, both that altar and the high place he brake down, and burned the high place, <hi type="italic">and</hi> stamped <hi type="italic">it</hi> small to powder, and burned the grove. <hi type="super">16</hi> And as Josiah turned himself, he spied the sepulchres that <hi type="italic">were</hi> there in the mount, and sent, and took the bones out of the sepulchres, and burned <hi type="italic">them</hi> upon the altar, and polluted it, according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which the man of God proclaimed, who proclaimed these words. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then he said, What title <hi type="italic">is</hi> that that I see? And the men of the city told him, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> the sepulchre of the man of God, which came from Judah, and proclaimed these things that thou hast done against the altar of Beth-el. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he said, Let him alone; let no man move his bones. So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet that came out of Samaria. <hi type="super">19</hi> And all the houses also of the high places that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the cities of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke <hi type="italic">the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> </hi> to anger, Josiah took away, and did to them according to all the acts that he had done in Beth-el. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he slew all the priests of the high places that <hi type="italic">were</hi> there upon the altars, and burned men's bones upon them, and returned to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the king commanded all the people, saying, Keep the passover unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written in the book of this covenant. <hi type="super">22</hi> Surely there was not holden such a passover from the days of the judges that judged Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel, nor of the kings of Judah; <hi type="super">23</hi> But in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, <hi type="italic">wherein</hi> this passover was holden to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">24</hi> Moreover the <hi type="italic">workers with</hi> familiar spirits, and the wizards, and the images, and the idols, and all the abominations that were spied in the land of Judah and in Jerusalem, did Josiah put away, that he might perform the words of the law which were written in the book that Hilkiah the priest found in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen7567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7568" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of such a reformation as we have not met with in all the history of the kings of Judah, such thorough riddance made of all the abominable things and such foundations laid of a glorious good work; and here I cannot but wonder at two things:—1. That so many wicked things should have got in, and kept standing so long, as we find here removed. 2. That notwithstanding the removal of these wicked things, and the hopeful prospects here given of a happy settlement, yet within a few years Jerusalem was utterly destroyed, and even this did not save it; for the generality of the people, after all, hated to be reformed. <hi type="italic">The founder melteth in vain,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">reprobate silver shall men call them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.29-Jer.6.30">Jer. vi. 29, 30</reference>. Let us here observe, <div eID="gen7568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7569" type="x-p"/> I. What abundance of wickedness there was, and had been, in Judah and Jerusalem. One would not have believed it possible that in Judah, where God was known—in Israel, where his name was great—in Salem, in Sion, where his dwelling place was, such abominations should be found as here we have an account of. Josiah had now reigned eighteen years, and had himself set the people a good example, and kept up religion according to law; and yet, when he came to make inquisition for idolatry, the depth and extent of the dunghill he had to carry away appeared almost incredible. 1. Even in the house of the Lord, that sacred temple which Solomon built, and dedicated to the honour and for the worship of the God of Israel, there were found vessels, all manner of utensils, for the worship of Baal, <hi type="italic">and of the grove</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi>), and <hi type="italic">of all the host of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">v. 4</reference>. Though Josiah had suppressed the worship of idols, yet the utensils made for that worship were all carefully preserved, even in the temple itself, to be used again whenever the present restraint should be taken off; nay, even the grove itself, the image of it, was yet standing in the temple (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">v. 6</reference>); some make it the image of Venus, the same with Ashtaroth. 2. Just <hi type="italic">at the entering in of the house of the Lord</hi> was a stable for horses kept (would you think it?) for a religious use; they were holy horses, <hi type="italic">given to the sun</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">v. 11</reference>), as if he needed them who <hi type="italic">rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.5">Ps. xix. 5</reference>), or rather they would thus represent to themselves the swiftness of his motion, which they much admired, making their religion to conform to the poetical fictions of the chariot of the sun, the follies of which even a little philosophy, without any divinity, would have exposed and made them ashamed of. Some say that those horses were to be led forth in pomp every morning to meet the rising sun, others that the worshippers of the sun rode out upon them to adore the rising sun; it should seem that they drew the chariots of the sun, which the people worshipped. Strange that ever men who had the written word of God among them should be thus <hi type="italic">vain in their imaginations!</hi> 3. Hard <hi type="italic">by the house of the Lord</hi> there were <hi type="italic">houses of the Sodomites,</hi> where all manner of lewdness and filthiness, even that which was most unnatural, was practised, and under pretence of religion too, in honour of their impure deities. Corporal and spiritual whoredom went together, and the vile affections to which the people were given up were the punishment of their vain imaginations. Those that dishonoured their God were justly left thus to dishonour themselves, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24-Rom.1.32">Rom. i. 24</reference>, &c. There were women that <hi type="italic">wove hangings for the grove</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.7">v. 7</reference>), tents which encompassed the image of Venus, where the worshippers committed all manner of lewdness, and this <hi type="italic">in the house of the Lord.</hi> Those did ill that made our Father's house a house of merchandise; those did worse that made it a den of thieves; but those did worst of all that made it (<hi type="italic">Horrendum dictu!</hi>—<hi type="italic">Horrible to relate!</hi>) a brothel, in an impudent defiance of the holiness of God and of his temple. Well might the apostle call them <hi type="italic">abominable idolatries.</hi> 4. There were many idolatrous altars found (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">v. 12</reference>), some in the palace, <hi type="italic">on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz.</hi> The roofs of their houses being flat, they made them their high places, and set up altars upon them (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">Jer. xix. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zeph. i. 5</reference>), domestic altars. The kings of Judah did so: and, though Josiah never used them, yet to this time they remained there. Manasseh had built altars for his idols in the house of the Lord. When he repented he removed them, and <hi type="italic">cast them out of the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.33.15">2 Chron. xxxiii. 15</reference>), but, not destroying them, his son Amon, it seems, had brought them again into the courts of the temple; there Josiah found them, and thence he <hi type="italic">broke them down,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.12">v. 12</reference>. 5. There was <hi type="italic">Tophet, in the valley of the son of Hinnom,</hi> very near Jerusalem, where the image of Moloch (that god of unnatural cruelty, as others were of unnatural uncleanness) was kept, to which some sacrificed their children, burning them in the fire, others dedicated them, making them to pass through the fire (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">labouring in the very fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Hab. ii. 13</reference>. It is supposed to have been called <hi type="italic">Tophet</hi> from <hi type="italic">toph,</hi> a drum, because they beat drums at the burning of the children, that their shrieks might not be heard. 6. There were <hi type="italic">high places before Jerusalem,</hi> which <hi type="italic">Solomon had built,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.13">v. 13</reference>. The altars and images on those high places, we may suppose, had been taken away by some of the preceding godly kings, or perhaps Solomon himself had removed them when he became a penitent; but the buildings, or some parts of them, remained, with other high places, till Josiah's time. Those that introduce corruptions into religion know not how far they will reach nor how long they will last. Antiquity is no certain proof of verity. There were also high places all the kingdom over, from <hi type="italic">Geba to Beer-sheba</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">v. 8</reference>), and <hi type="italic">high places of the gates, in the entering in of the gate of the governor.</hi> In these high places (bishop Patrick thinks) they burnt incense to those tutelar gods to whom their idolatrous kings had committed the protection of their city; and probably the governor of the city had a private altar for his <hi type="italic">penates</hi>—<hi type="italic">his household-gods.</hi> 7. There were idolatrous priests, that officiated at all those idolatrous altars (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">v. 5</reference>), chemarim, black men, or that wore black. See <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.4">Zeph. i. 4</reference>. Those that sacrificed to Osiris, or that wept for Tammuz (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.14">Ezek. viii. 14</reference>), or that worshipped the infernal deities, put on black garments as mourners. These idolatrous priests the kings of <hi type="italic">Judah had ordained to burn incense in the high places;</hi> they were, it should seem, priests of the house of Aaron, who thus profaned their dignity, and there were others also who had no right at all to the priesthood, who burnt incense to Baal. 8. There were conjurers and wizards, and such as <hi type="italic">dealt with familiar spirits,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.24">v. 24</reference>. When they worshipped the devil as their god no marvel that they consulted him as their oracle. <div eID="gen7569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7570" type="x-p"/> II. What a full destruction good Josiah made of all those relics of idolatry. Such is his zeal for the Lord of hosts, and his holy indignation against all that is displeasing to him, that nothing shall stand before him. The law was that the monuments of the Canaanites' idolatry must be all destroyed (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.5">Deut. vii. 5</reference>), much more those of the idolatry of the Israelites, in whom it was much more impious, profane, and perfidious. 1. He ordered Hilkiah, and the other priests, to clear the temple. This was their province, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4">v. 4</reference>. Away with all the vessels that were made for Baal. They must never be employed in the service of God, no, nor reserved for any common use; they must all be burnt, and the ashes of them carried to Bethel. That place had been the common source of idolatry, for there was set up one of the calves, and, that lying next to Judah, the infection had thence spread into that kingdom, and therefore Josiah made it the lay-stall of idolatry, the dunghill to which he carried the filth and offscouring of all things, that, if possible, it might be made loathsome to those that had been fond of it. 2. The idolatrous priests were all put down. Those of them that were not of the house of Aaron, or had sacrificed to Baal or other false gods, he put to death, according to the law, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.20">v. 20</reference>. He <hi type="italic">slew them upon their own altars,</hi> the most acceptable sacrifice that ever had been offered upon them, a sacrifice to the justice of God. Those that were descendants from Aaron, and yet had burnt incense in the high places, but to the true God only, he forbade ever to approach the altar of the Lord; they had forfeited that honour (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.9">v. 9</reference>): He <hi type="italic">brought them out of the cities of Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">v. 8</reference>), that they might not do mischief in the country by secretly keeping up their old idolatrous usages; but he allowed them to <hi type="italic">eat of the unleavened bread</hi> (the bread of the meat-offering, <reference osisRef="Lev.2.4-Lev.2.5">Lev. ii. 4, 5</reference>) <hi type="italic">among their brethren,</hi> with whom they were to reside, that being under their eye they might be kept from doing hurt and taught to do well; that bread, that unleavened bread (heavy and unpleasant as it was), was better than they deserved, and that would serve to keep them alive. But whether they were permitted to eat of all the sacrifices, as blemished priests were (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.22">Lev. xxi. 22</reference>), which is called, in general, <hi type="italic">the bread of their God,</hi> may be justly questioned. 3. All the images were broken to pieces and burnt. The image of the grove (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">v. 6</reference>), some goddess or other, was reduced to ashes, and the <hi type="italic">ashes cast upon the graves of the common people</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">v. 6</reference>), the common burying-place of the city. By the law a ceremonial uncleanness was contracted by the touch of a grave, so that in casting them here he declared them most impure, and none could touch them without thereby making themselves unclean. <hi type="italic">He cast it into the graves</hi> (so the Chaldee), intimating that he would have all idolatry buried out of his sight, as a loathsome thing, and forgotten, as dead men are out of mind, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.14">v. 14</reference>. He <hi type="italic">filled the places of the groves with the bones of men;</hi> as he carried the ashes of the images to the graves, to mingle them with dead men's bones, so he carried dead men's bones to the places where the images had been, and put them in the room of them, that, both ways, idolatry might be rendered loathsome, and the people kept both from the dust of the images and from the ruins of the places where they had been worshipped. Dead men and dead gods were much alike and fittest to go together. 4. All the wicked houses were suppressed, those nests of impiety that harboured idolaters, the houses of the Sodomites, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.7">v. 7</reference>. "Down with them, down with them, rase them to the foundations." The high places were in like manner broken down and levelled with the ground (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">v. 8</reference>), even that which belonged to the governor of the city; for no man's greatness or power may protect him in idolatry or profaneness. Let governors be obliged, in the first place, to reform, and then the governed will be the sooner influenced. He defiled the high places (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.8">v. 8</reference> and again <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.13">v. 13</reference>), did all he could to render them abominable, and put the people out of conceit with them, as Jehu did when he made the house of Baal a draught-house, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.27">2 Kings x. 27</reference>. Tophet, which, contrary to other places of idolatry, was in a valley, whereas they were on hills or high places, was likewise defiled (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">v. 10</reference>), was made the burying-place of the city. Concerning this we have a whole sermon, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1-Jer.19.15">Jer. xix. 1, 2</reference>, &c., where it is said, <hi type="italic">They shall bury in Tophet,</hi> and the whole city is threatened to be made like Tophet. 5. The horses that had been given to the sun were taken away and put to common use, and so were delivered from the vanity to which they were made subject; and the chariots of the sun (what a pity was it that those horses and chariots should be kept as the chariots and horsemen of Israel!) he burnt with fire; and, if the sun be a flame, they never resembled him so much as they did when they were chariots of fire. 6. The workers with familiar spirits and the wizards were put away, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.24">v. 24</reference>. Those of them that were convicted of witchcraft, it is likely, he put to death, and so deterred others from those diabolical practices. In all this he had a sincere regard to <hi type="italic">the words of the law which were written in the book</hi> lately found, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.24">v. 24</reference>. He made that law his rule and kept that in his eye throughout this reformation. <div eID="gen7570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7571" type="x-p"/> III. How his zeal extended itself to the cities of Israel that were within his reach. The ten tribes were carried captive and the Assyrian colonies did not fully people the country, so that, it is likely, many cities had put themselves under the protection of the kings of Judah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.1">2 Chron. xxx. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.6">xxxiv. 6</reference>. These he here visits, to carry on his reformation. As far as our influence goes our endeavours should go to do good and bring the wickedness of the wicked to an end. <div eID="gen7571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7572" type="x-p"/> 1. He defiled and demolished Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, with the high place and the grove that belonged to it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.15-2Kgs.23.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. The golden calf, it should seem, was gone (<hi type="italic">thy calf, O Samaria! has cast thee off</hi>), but the altar was there, which those that were wedded to their old idolatries made use of still. This was, (1.) Defiled, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.16">v. 16</reference>. Josiah, in his pious zeal, was ransacking the old seats of idolatry, and spied the sepulchres in the mount, in which probably the idolatrous priests were buried, not far from the altar at which they had officiated, and which they were so fond of that they were desirous to lay their bones by it; these he opened, took out the bones, and <hi type="italic">burnt them upon the altar,</hi> to show that thus he would have done by the priests themselves if they had been alive, as he did by those whom he found alive, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.20">v. 20</reference>. Thus he polluted the altar, desecrated it, and made it odious. It is threatened against idolaters (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.1-Jer.8.2">Jer. viii. 1, 2</reference>) that <hi type="italic">their bones shall be spread before the sun;</hi> that which is there threatened and this which is here executed (bespeaking their <hi type="italic">iniquity to be upon their bones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Ezek. xxxii. 27</reference>) are an intimation of a punishment after death, reserved for those that live and die impenitent in that or any other sin; the burning of the bones, if that were all, is a small matter, but, if it signify the torment of the soul in a worse flame (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.24">Luke xvi. 24</reference>), it is very dreadful. This, as it was Josiah's act, seems to have been the result of a very sudden resolve; he would not have done it but that he happened to turn himself, and spy the sepulchres; and yet it was foretold above 350 years before, when this altar was first built by Jeroboam, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">1 Kings xiii. 2</reference>. God always foresees, and has sometimes foretold as certain, that which yet to us seems most contingent. <hi type="italic">The king's heart is in the hand of the Lord;</hi> king Josiah's was so, and he turned it (or ever he himself was aware, <reference osisRef="Song.6.12">Cant. vi. 12</reference>) to do this. No work of God shall fall to the ground. (2.) It was demolished. He broke down the altar and all its appurtenances (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.15">v. 15</reference>), burnt what was combustible, and, since an idol is nothing in the world, he went as far towards the annihilating of it as he could; for he <hi type="italic">stamped it small to powder</hi> and made it <hi type="italic">as dust before the wind.</hi> <div eID="gen7572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7573" type="x-p"/> 2. He destroyed all the houses of the high places, all those synagogues of Satan that were <hi type="italic">in the cities of Samaria,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.19">v. 19</reference>. These the kings of Israel built, and God raised up this king of Judah to pull them down, for the honour of the ancient house of David, from which the ten tribes had revolted; the priests he justly made sacrifices <hi type="italic">upon their own altars,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.20">v. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen7573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7574" type="x-p"/> 3. He carefully preserved the sepulchre of that man of God who came from Judah to foretel this, which now a king who came from Judah executed. This was that good prophet who <hi type="italic">proclaimed these things against the altar of Bethel,</hi> and yet was himself slain by a lion for disobeying the word of the Lord; but to show that God's displeasure against him went no further than his death, but ended there, God so ordered it that when all the graves about his were disturbed his was safe (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.17-2Kgs.23.18">v. 17, 18</reference>) and no man moved his bones. He had entered into peace, and therefore should rest in his bed, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa. lvii. 2</reference>. The old lying prophet, who desired to be buried as near him as might be, it should seem, knew what he did; for his dust also, being mingled with that of the good prophet, was preserved for his sake; see <reference osisRef="Num.23.10">Num. xxiii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen7574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7575" type="x-p"/> IV. We are here told what a solemn passover Josiah and his people kept after all this. When they had cleared the country of the old leaven they then applied themselves to the keeping of the feast. When Jehu had destroyed the worship of Baal, yet he took no heed to walk in the commandments and ordinances of God; but Josiah considered that we must learn to do well, and no <hi type="italic">only</hi> cease to do evil, and that the way to keep out all abominable customs is to keep up all instituted ordinances (see <reference osisRef="Lev.18.30">Lev. xviii. 30</reference>), and therefore he commanded all the people to keep the passover, which was not only a memorial of their deliverance out of Egypt, but a token of their dedication to him that brought them out and their communion with him. This he found written in the <hi type="italic">book of the law,</hi> here called <hi type="italic">the book of the covenant;</hi> for, though the divine authority may deal with us in a way of absolute command, divine grace condescends to federal transactions, and therefore he observed it. We have not such a particular account of this passover as of that in Hezekiah's time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.1-2Chr.30.27">2 Chron. xxx.</reference> But, in general, we are told that <hi type="italic">there was not holden such a passover</hi> in any of the foregoing reigns, no, not <hi type="italic">from the days of the judges</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.22">v. 22</reference>), which, by the way, intimates that, though the account which the book of Judges gives of the state of Israel under that dynasty looks but melancholy, yet there were then some golden days. This passover, it seems, was extraordinary for the number and devotion of the communicants, their sacrifices and offerings, and their exact observance of the laws of the feast; and it was not now as in Hezekiah's passover, when many communicated that were not cleansed according to the purification of the sanctuary, and the Levites were permitted to do the priests' work. We have reason to think that during all the remainder of Josiah's reign religion flourished and the feasts of the Lord were very carefully observed; but in this passover the satisfaction they took in the covenant lately renewed, the reformation in pursuance of it, and the revival of an ordinance of which they had lately found the divine original in the book of the law, and which had long been neglected or carelessly kept, put them into great transports of holy joy; and God was pleased to recompense their zeal in destroying idolatry with uncommon tokens of his presence and favour. All this concurred to make it a distinguished passover.
entries.b17b550e82eda10af5bede1cd93ba85cc689adc9: <div eID="gen7575" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of Josiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 610.)</title> <div sID="gen7576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there <hi type="italic">any</hi> like him. <hi type="super">26</hi> Notwithstanding the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> turned not from the fierceness of his great wrath, wherewith his anger was kindled against Judah, because of all the provocations that Manasseh had provoked him withal. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, I will remove Judah also out of my sight, as I have removed Israel, and will cast off this city Jerusalem which I have chosen, and the house of which I said, My name shall be there. <hi type="super">28</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Josiah, and all that he did, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? <hi type="super">29</hi> In his days Pharaoh-nechoh king of Egypt went up against the king of Assyria to the river Euphrates: and king Josiah went against him; and he slew him at Megiddo, when he had seen him. <hi type="super">30</hi> And his servants carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo, and brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own sepulchre. And the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father's stead. <div eID="gen7576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7577" type="x-p"/> Upon the reading of these verses we must say, Lord, though <hi type="italic">thy righteousness</hi> be <hi type="italic">as the great mountains</hi>—evident, conspicuous, and past dispute, yet <hi type="italic">thy judgments are a great deep,</hi> unfathomable and past finding out, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Ps. xxxvi. 6</reference>. What shall we say to this? <div eID="gen7577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7578" type="x-p"/> I. It is here owned that Josiah was one of the best kings that ever sat upon the throne of David, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.25">v. 25</reference>. As Hezekiah was a non-such for faith and dependence upon God in straits (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.5">ch. xviii. 5</reference>), so Josiah was a non-such for sincerity and zeal in carrying on a work of reformation. For this there was none like him, 1. That he <hi type="italic">turned to the Lord</hi> from whom his fathers had revolted. It is true religion to turn to God as one we have chosen and love. He did what he could to turn his kingdom also to the Lord. 2. That he did this <hi type="italic">with his heart and soul;</hi> his affections and aims were right in what he did. Those make nothing of their religion that do not make heart-work of it. 3. That he did it with <hi type="italic">all his heart,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all his soul,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all his might</hi>—with vigour, and courage, and resolution: he could not otherwise have broken through the difficulties he had to grapple with. What great things may we bring to pass in the service of God if we be but lively and hearty in it! 4. That he did this <hi type="italic">according to all the law of Moses,</hi> in an exact observance of that law and with an actual regard to it. His zeal did not transport him into any irregularities, but, in all he did, he walked by rule. <div eID="gen7578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7579" type="x-p"/> II. Notwithstanding this he was cut off by a violent death in the midst of his days, and his kingdom was ruined within a few years after. Consequent upon such a reformation as this, one would have expected nothing but the prosperity and glory both of king and kingdom; but, quite contrary, we find both under a cloud. 1. Even the reformed kingdom continues marked for ruin. For all this (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.26">v. 26</reference>) <hi type="italic">the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his great wrath.</hi> That is certainly true, which God spoke by the prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.7-Jer.18.8">Jer. xviii. 7, 8</reference>), that if a nation, doomed to destruction, <hi type="italic">turn from the evil</hi> of sin, God will <hi type="italic">repent of the evil</hi> of punishment; and therefore we must conclude that Josiah's people, though they submitted to Josiah's power, did not heartily imbibe Josiah's principles. They were turned by force, and did not voluntarily <hi type="italic">turn from their evil way,</hi> but still continued their affection for their idols; and therefore he that knows men's hearts would not recall the sentence, which was, That Judah should be removed, as Israel had been, and Jerusalem itself cast off, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">v. 27</reference>. Yet even this destruction was intended to be their effectual reformation; so that we must say, not only that the criminals had filled their measure and were ripe for ruin, but also that the disease had come to a crisis, and was ready for a cure; and this shall be all the fruit, even the taking away of sin. 2. As an evidence of this, even the reforming king is cut off in the midst of his usefulness—in mercy to him, that he might not see the evil which was coming upon his kingdom, but in wrath to his people, for his death was an inlet to their desolations. The king of Egypt waged war, it seems, with the king of Assyria: so the king of Babylon is now called. Josiah's kingdom lay between them. He therefore thought himself concerned to oppose the king of Egypt, and check the growing, threatening, greatness of his power; for though, at this time, he protested that he had no design against Josiah, yet, if he should prevail to unite the river of Egypt and the river Euphrates, the land of Judah would soon be overflowed between them. Therefore <hi type="italic">Josiah went against him,</hi> and was killed in the first engagement, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29-2Kgs.23.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. Here, (1.) We cannot justify Josiah's conduct. He had no clear call to engage in this war, nor do we find that he asked counsel of God by urim or prophets concerning it. What had he to do to appear and act as a friend and ally to the king of Assyria? <hi type="italic">Should he help the ungodly and love those that hate the Lord?</hi> If the kings of Egypt and Assyria quarrelled, he had reason to think God would bring good out of it to him and his people, by making them instrumental to weaken one another. Some understand the promise made to him that he should <hi type="italic">come to his grave in peace</hi> in a sense in which it was not performed because, by his miscarriage in this matter, he forfeited the benefit of it. God has promised to keep us <hi type="italic">in all our ways;</hi> but, if we go out of our way, we throw ourselves out of his protection. I understand the promise so as that I believe it was fulfilled, for he <hi type="italic">died in peace</hi> with God and his own conscience, and saw not, nor had any immediate prospect of, the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans; yet I understand the providence to be a rebuke to him for his rashness. (2.) We must adore God's righteousness in taking away such a jewel from an unthankful people that knew not how to value it. They greatly lamented his death (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2 Chron. xxxv. 25</reference>), urged to it by Jeremiah, who told them the meaning of it, and what a threatening omen it was; but they had not made a due improvement of the mercies they enjoyed by his life, of which God taught them the worth by the want.
entries.e7e33705f667fbbf588fe0da24b560a1b5cfa46d: <div eID="gen7579" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Reigns of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 610.)</title> <div sID="gen7580" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Jehoahaz <hi type="italic">was</hi> twenty and three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , according to all that his fathers had done. <hi type="super">33</hi> And Pharaoh-nechoh put him in bands at Riblah in the land of Hamath, that he might not reign in Jerusalem; and put the land to a tribute of a hundred talents of silver, and a talent of gold. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Pharaoh-nechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there. <hi type="super">35</hi> And Jehoiakim gave the silver and the gold to Pharaoh; but he taxed the land to give the money according to the commandment of Pharaoh: he exacted the silver and the gold of the people of the land, of every one according to his taxation, to give <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto Pharaoh-nechoh. <hi type="super">36</hi> Jehoiakim <hi type="italic">was</hi> twenty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. <hi type="super">37</hi> And he did <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , according to all that his fathers had done. <div eID="gen7580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7581" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem saw not a good day after Josiah was laid in his grave, but one trouble came after another, till within twenty-two years it was quite destroyed. Of the reign of two of his sons here is a short account; the former we find here a prisoner and the latter a tributary to the king of Egypt, and both so in the very beginning of their reign. This king of Egypt having slain Josiah, though he had not had any design upon Judah, yet, being provoked by the opposition which Josiah gave him, now, it should seem, he bent all his force against his family and kingdom. If Josiah's sons had trodden in his steps, they would have fared the better for his piety; but, deviating from them, they fared the worse for his rashness. <div eID="gen7581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7582" type="x-p"/> I. Jehoahaz, a younger son, was first made king by <hi type="italic">the people of the land,</hi> probably because he was observed to be of a more active warlike genius than his elder brother, and likely to make head against the king of Egypt and to avenge his father's death, which perhaps the people were more solicitous about, in point of honour, than the keeping up and carrying on of his father's reformation; and the issue was accordingly. 1. He did ill, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.32">v. 32</reference>. Though he had a good education and a good example given him, and many a good prayer, we may suppose, put up for him, yet he <hi type="italic">did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord,</hi> and, it is to be feared, began to do so in his father's lifetime, for his reign was so short that he could not, in that, show much of his character. He did <hi type="italic">according to all that his</hi> wicked <hi type="italic">fathers had done.</hi> Though he had not time to do much, yet he had chosen his patterns, and showed whom he intended to follow and whose steps he resolved to tread in; and, having done this, he is here reckoned to have done according to all the evil which those did whom he proposed to imitate. It is of great consequence to young people whom they choose to take for their patterns and whom they emulate. An error in this choice is fatal. <reference osisRef="Phil.3.17-Phil.3.18">Phil. iii. 17, 18</reference>. 2. Doing ill, no wonder that he fared ill. He was but three months a prince, and was then made a prisoner, and lived and died so. The king of Egypt seized him, and put him in bands (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33">v. 33</reference>), fearing lest he should give him disturbance, and carried him to Egypt, where he died soon after, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.34">v. 34</reference>. This Jehoahaz is that young lion whom Ezekiel speaks of in his <hi type="italic">lamentation for the princes of Israel,</hi> that learnt to <hi type="italic">catch the prey and devour men</hi> (that was the evil which he did in the sight of the Lord); but <hi type="italic">the nations heard of him, he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains into the land of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.1-Ezek.19.4">Ezek. xix. 1-4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jer.22.10-Jer.22.12">Jer. xxii. 10-12</reference>. <div eID="gen7582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7583" type="x-p"/> II. Eliakim, another son of Josiah, was made king by the king of Egypt, it is not said <hi type="italic">in the room of Jehoahaz</hi> (his reign was so short that it was scarcely worth taking notice of), but <hi type="italic">in the room of Josiah.</hi> The crown of Judah had hitherto always descended from a father to a son, and never, till now, from one brother to another; once the succession had so happened in the house of Ahab, but never, till now, in the house of David. The king of Egypt, having used his power in making him king, further showed it in changing his name; he called him <hi type="italic">Jehoiakim,</hi> a name that has reference to Jehovah, for he had no design to make him renounce or forget the religion of his country. "All people will walk in the name of their God, and let him do so." The king of Babylon did not do so by those whose names he changed, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.7">Dan. i. 7</reference>. Of this Jehoiakim we are here told, 1. That the king of Egypt made him poor, exacted from him a vast tribute of 100 <hi type="italic">talents of silver and a talent of gold</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33">v. 33</reference>), which, with much difficulty, he squeezed out of his subjects and gave to Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.35">v. 35</reference>. Formerly the Israelites had spoiled the Egyptians; now the Egyptians spoil Israel. See what woeful changes sin makes. 2. That which made him poor, yet did not make him good. Notwithstanding the rebukes of Providence he was under, by which he should have been convinced, humbled, and reformed, he <hi type="italic">did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.37">v. 37</reference>), and so prepared against himself greater judgments; for such God will send if less do not do the work for which they are sent.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.23"/> <div eID="gen7583" type="x-p"/>

entries.03e6e8c08be641639598cc681b075adc4a3a5d3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3577"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <div sID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.1-2Kgs.23.3">2Ki 23:1-3</reference>. Josiah Causes the Law to Be Read.<div eID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3577"/><hi type="bold">1-3. the king sent, and they gathered unto him all the elders--</hi>This pious and patriotic king, not content with the promise of his own security, felt, after Huldah's response, an increased desire to avert the threatened calamities from his kingdom and people. Knowing the richness of the divine clemency and grace to the penitent, he convened the elders of the people, and placing himself at their head, accompanied by the collective body of the inhabitants, went in solemn procession to the temple, where he ordered the book of the law to be read to the assembled audience, and covenanted, with the unanimous concurrence of his subjects, to adhere steadfastly to all the commandments of the Lord. It was an occasion of solemn interest, closely connected with a great national crisis, and the beautiful example of piety in the highest quarter would exert a salutary influence over all classes of the people in animating their devotions and encouraging their return to the faith of their fathers. <div eID="gen5095" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8bfe65c6c0d21d86e3c7cf18aa952563c0df6e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3580"/><div sID="gen5099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3580"/><hi type="bold">4. the king commanded Hilkiah, &c.--</hi>that is, the high priest and other priests, for there was not a variety of official gradations in the temple.<div eID="gen5099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the vessels, &c.--</hi>the whole apparatus of idol-worship.<div eID="gen5100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burned them without Jerusalem--</hi>The law required them to be consigned to the flames (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.25">De 7:25</reference>).<div eID="gen5101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the fields of Kidron--</hi>most probably that part of the valley of Kidron, where lies Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. It is a level, spacious basin, abounding at present with plantations [Robinson]. The brook winds along the east and south of the city, the channel of which is throughout a large portion of the year almost or wholly dry, except after heavy rains, when it suddenly swells and overflows. There were emptied all the impurities of the temple (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.15">2Ch 29:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.16">16</reference>) and the city. His reforming predecessors had ordered the mutilated relics of idolatry to be thrown into that receptacle of filth (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.13">1Ki 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2Ch 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.14">30:14</reference>); but Josiah, while he imitated their piety, far outstripped them in zeal; for he caused the ashes of the burnt wood and the fragments of the broken metal to be collected and conveyed to Beth-el, in order thenceforth to associate ideas of horror and aversion with that place, as odious for the worst pollutions. <div eID="gen5102" type="x-p"/>
entries.240a5f0f6ab1fc24acc4fff73315a83a7840ba79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3581"/><div sID="gen5103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3581"/><hi type="bold">5. put down the idolatrous priests--</hi>Hebrew, chemarim, "scorched," that is, Guebres, or fire-worshippers, distinguished by a girdle (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.14-Ezek.23.17">Eze 23:14-17</reference>) or belt of wool and camel's hair, twisted round the body twice and tied with four knots, which had a symbolic meaning, and made it a supposed defense against evil.<div eID="gen5103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them also that burned incense unto Baal, to the sun, and to the moon, &c.--</hi>or Baal-shemesh, for Baal was sometimes considered the sun. This form of false worship was not by images, but pure star-worship, borrowed from the old Assyrians.<div eID="gen5104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and--</hi>rather, "even to all the host of heaven." <div eID="gen5105" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1c1c0aa73f9ba166408ba002c0bbf83e4c6f5e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3582"/><div sID="gen5106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3582"/><hi type="bold">6. brought out the grove--</hi>that is, Asherah, the mystic tree, placed by Manasseh in the temple [2Ki 21:5; 2Ch 33:5], removed by him after his conversion [2Ch 33:15], but replaced in the sanctuary by his wicked son Amon [2Ki 21:20, 21]. Josiah had it taken to Kidron, burnt the wood, ground the metal about it to powder, and strewed the ashes "on the graves of the children of the people." The poor were buried in a common on part of the valley of Kidron. But reference is here made to the graves "of those that had sacrificed" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>). <div eID="gen5106" type="x-p"/>
entries.73494a65bebaf98418866b05b406325295f77202: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3583"/><div sID="gen5107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3583"/><hi type="bold">7. brake down the houses of the sodomites--</hi>not solid houses, but tents, called elsewhere [2Ki 17:30] Succoth-benoth, "the booths of the young women," who were devoted to the service of Asherah, for which they made embroidered hangings, and in which they gave themselves to unbridled revelry and lust. Or the hangings might be for Asherah itself, as it is a popular superstition in the East to hang pieces of cloth on trees. <div eID="gen5107" type="x-p"/>
entries.dacd95b8f87884a2a3620a67562d18a445565270: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3584"/><div sID="gen5108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3584"/><hi type="bold">8-9. he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places, &c.--</hi>Many of the Levitical order, finding in the reigns of Manasseh and Amon the temple-worship abolished and the tithes and other offerings alienated, had been betrayed into the folly of officiating on high places, and presenting such sacrifices as were brought to them. These irregularities, even though the object of that worship was the true God, were prohibited in the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">De 12:11</reference>). Those who had been guilty of this sin, Josiah brought to Jerusalem. Regarding them as defiled, he debarred them from the service of the temple, but gave them an allowance out of the temple revenues, like the lame and disabled members of the priesthood (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.21">Le 21:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen5108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Geba to to Beer-sheba--</hi>the most northern and the most southern places in Judah--meaning all parts of the kingdom.<div eID="gen5109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the high places ... which were in the entering in of the gate of Joshua--</hi>The governor's house and gate were on the left of the city gate, and close by the entrance of that civic mansion house were public altars, dedicated, it might be, to the true God, but contrary to His own ordinance of worship (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.8">Is 57:8</reference>). <div eID="gen5110" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c2d6d21bca395984a3b51a833422e1c1cf2e3fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3585"/><div sID="gen5111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3585"/><hi type="bold">10. Topheth--</hi>so called from Toph--a "drum." It is the prevailing opinion among Jewish writers that the cries of the terrified children made to pass through the fire in that place of idolatrous horror were drowned by the sound of that instrument. <div eID="gen5111" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c5531b835e5ffc65e70f72396633ceed31aebf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3586"/><div sID="gen5112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3586"/><hi type="bold">11. took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun--</hi>Among the people who anciently worshipped the sun, horses were usually dedicated to that divinity, from the supposed idea that the sun himself was drawn in a chariot by horses. In some cases these horses were sacrificed; but more commonly they were employed either in the sacred processions to carry the images of the sun, or for the worshippers to ride in every morning to welcome his rise. It seems that the idolatrous kings, Ahaz, Manasseh, and Amon, or their great officers, proceeded on these horses early on each day from the east gate of the temple to salute and worship the sun at his appearing above the horizon. <div eID="gen5112" type="x-p"/>
entries.70fa65f2f59467292591e1da9de074bdff510f1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3587"/><div sID="gen5113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3587"/><hi type="bold">12. the altars that were on the top of the upper chamber of Ahaz--</hi>Altars were reared on the flat roofs of houses, where the worshippers of "the host of heaven" burnt incense (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zep 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">Jr 19:13</reference>). Ahaz had reared altars for this purpose on the oleah, or upper chamber of his palace, and Manasseh on some portion of the roof of the temple. Josiah demolished both of these structures. <div eID="gen5113" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e6421727488838ba2e3cd9ab9d6606f5d3b6db3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3588"/><div sID="gen5114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3588"/><hi type="bold">13-14. the high places ... which Solomon ... had builded--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5">1Ki 11:5</reference>).<div eID="gen5114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the right hand of the mount of corruption--</hi>The Mount of Olives is a hilly range on the east of Jerusalem. This range has three summits, of which the central one is the Mount of Corruption, so called from the idol temples built there, and of course the hill on the right hand denotes the southernmost peak. Josiah is said not to have destroyed, but only defiled, "the high places on the hill of corruption." It is most probable that Hezekiah had long before demolished the idolatrous temples erected there by Solomon but, as the superstitious people continued to regard the spot as consecrated ground, Josiah defiled it. <div eID="gen5115" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fb57f83925d5add92b3378cd3f587c2e5742745: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3590"/><div sID="gen5117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3590"/><hi type="bold">15-20. Moreover the altar that was at Beth-el, &c.--</hi>Not satisfied with the removal of every vestige of idolatry from his own dominion, this zealous iconoclast made a tour of inspection through the cities of Samaria and all the territory formerly occupied by the ten tribes, destroying the altars and temples of the high places, consigning the Asherim to the flames, putting to death the priests of the high places, and showing his horror at idolatry by ransacking the sepulchers of idolatrous priests, and strewing the burnt ashes of their bones upon the altars before he demolished them. <div eID="gen5117" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb65a1c4f855201807803ff3b2edfc36d9079a01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3593"/><div sID="gen5121" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3593"/><hi type="bold">21-23. the king commanded all the people, saying, Keep the passover unto the Lord your God, &c.--</hi>It was observed with great solemnity and was attended not only by his own subjects, but by the remnant people from Israel (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.1-2Chr.35.19">2Ch 35:1-19</reference>). Many of the Israelites who were at Jerusalem might have heard of, if they did not hear, the law read by Josiah. It is probable that they might even have procured a copy of the law, stimulated as they were to the better observance of Jehovah's worship by the unusual and solemn transactions at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen5121" type="x-p"/>
entries.97ccd3dea02486e5d44a7ebb30e01834b78fb854: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3594"/><div sID="gen5122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3594"/><hi type="bold">26. Notwithstanding, the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his wrath,--</hi>&c. The national reformation which Josiah carried on was acquiesced in by the people from submission to the royal will; but they entertained a secret and strong hankering after the suppressed idolatries. Though outwardly purified, their hearts were not right towards God, as appears from many passages of the prophetic writings; their thorough reform was hopeless; and God, who saw no sign of genuine repentance, allowed His decree (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.12-2Kgs.21.15">2Ki 21:12-15</reference>) for the subversion of the kingdom to take fatal effect. <div eID="gen5122" type="x-p"/>
entries.c88936c9e637eb826b90defdb2957a23dd817244: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3595"/><div sID="gen5123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3595"/><hi type="bold">29. In his days Pharaoh-nechoh--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.20-2Chr.35.27">2Ch 35:20-27</reference>). <chapter eID="2Kgs.23"/>

entries.4fabcc96fba144c4eee29063bf4097a47940688e: <div eID="gen13236" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13237" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13238" type="x-p"/> Josiah reads in the temple to the elders of Judah, the priests, the prophets, and the people, the book of the covenant which had been found, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.1">2Kgs 23:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.2">2Kgs 23:2</reference>. He makes a covenant, and the people stand to it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.3">2Kgs 23:3</reference>. He destroys the vessels of Baal and Asherah, and puts down the idolatrous priests; breaks down the houses of the sodomites, and the high places; defiles Topheth; takes away the horses of the sun; destroys the altars of Ahaz; breaks in pieces the images; and breaks down and burns Jeroboam's altar at Beth-el, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.4-2Kgs.23.15">2Kgs 23:4-15</reference>. Fulfills the word of the prophet, who cried against the altar at Beth-el, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.16-2Kgs.23.18">2Kgs 23:16-18</reference>. Destroys the high places in Samaria, slays the idolatrous priests, and celebrates a great passover, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.19-2Kgs.23.23">2Kgs 23:19-23</reference>; and puts away all the dealers with familiar spirits, etc., <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.24">2Kgs 23:24</reference>. His eminent character; he is mortally wounded at Megiddo, and buried at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.25-2Kgs.23.30">2Kgs 23:25-30</reference>. Jehoahaz reigns in his stead, and does evil in the sight of the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31">2Kgs 23:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.32">2Kgs 23:32</reference>. Is dethroned by Pharaoh-nechoh; and Eliakim, his brother, called also Jehoiakim, made king in his stead; the land is laid under tribute by the king of Egypt, and Jehoiakim reigns wickedly, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.33-2Kgs.23.37">2Kgs 23:33-37</reference>.
entries.64b7c0864e00c17b5177a25c8bb6a6be9bb4718e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13238" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13237" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13239" type="x-p"/> The king went up into the house of the Lord - Here is another very singular circumstance. The high priest, scribes, priest, and prophets, are gathered together, with all the elders of the people, and the king himself reads the book of the covenant which had been lately found! It is strange that either the high priest, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, or some other of the prophets, who were certainly there present, did not read the sacred book! It is likely that the king considered himself a mediator between God and them, and therefore read and made the covenant.
entries.1bc86a7549c617484e693fe2fac237dbe704c025: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13240" type="x-p"/> Stood by a pillar - He stood, על העמוד al haammud, "upon the stairs or pulpit." This is what is called the brazen scaffold or pulpit which Solomon made, and on which the kings were accustomed to stand when they addressed the people. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.13">2Chr 6:13</reference>, and the parallel places. <div eID="gen13240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13241" type="x-p"/> Made a covenant - This was expressed, <div eID="gen13241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13242" type="x-p"/> 1. In general. To walk after Jehovah; to have no gods besides him. <div eID="gen13242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13243" type="x-p"/> 2. To take his law for the regulation of their conduct. <div eID="gen13243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13244" type="x-p"/> 3. In particular. To bend their whole heart and soul to the observance of it, so that, they might not only have religion without, but, piety within. <div eID="gen13244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13245" type="x-p"/> To this all the people stood up, thus giving their consent, and binding themselves to obedience.
entries.7e24f415ae1230ca88ed25aa0498f44eee6c978e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen13245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13246" type="x-p"/> The priests of the second order - These were probably such as supplied the place of the high priest when he was prevented: from fulfilling the functions of his office. So the Chaldee understood the place - the sagan of the high priests. But the words may refer to those of the second course or order established by David: though it does not appear that those orders were now in use, yet the distinction was continued even to the time of our Lord. We find the course of Abia, which was the eighth, mentioned <reference osisRef="Luk.1.5">Luk 1:5</reference> (note); where see the note. <div eID="gen13246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13247" type="x-p"/> All the vessels - These had been used for idolatrous purposes; the king is now to destroy them; for although no longer used in this way, they might, if permitted to remain, be an incentive to idolatry at a future time.
entries.0b2860b593fb3b3a5a2373f3bdf2d77fa4297184: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen13247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13248" type="x-p"/> The idolatrous priests - הכמרים hakkemarim. Who these were is not well known. The Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic, call them the priests simply, which the kings of Judah had ordained. Probably they were an order made by the idolatrous kings of Judah, and called kemarim, from כמר camar, which signifies to be scorched, shriveled together, made dark, or black, because their business was constantly to attend sacrificial fires, and probably they were black garments; hence the Jews in derision call Christian ministers kemarim, because of their black clothes and garments. Why we should imitate, in our sacerdotal dress, those priests of Baal, is strange to think and hard to tell. <div eID="gen13248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13249" type="x-p"/> Unto Baal, to the sun - Though Baal was certainly the sun, yet here they are distinguished; Baal being worshipped under different forms and attributes, Baal-peor, Baal-zephon, Baal-zebub, etc. <div eID="gen13249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13250" type="x-p"/> The planets - מזלות mazzaloth. The Vulgate translates this the twelve signs, i.e., the zodiac. This is as likely as any of the other conjectures which have been published relative to this word. See a similar word <reference osisRef="Job.37.9">Job 37:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.32">Job 38:32</reference>.
entries.f9f5bab119dd91666d59673571a27cdb1102ac4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen13250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> He brought out the grove - He brought out the idol Asherah. See at the end of <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.26">2Kgs 21:26</reference> (note). <div eID="gen13251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13252" type="x-p"/> Upon the graves of the children of the people - I believe this; means the burial-place of the common people.
entries.f281ee24f3be326a4682d3e73e28d601d00b7671: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen13252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> The houses of the sodomites - We have already often met with these קדשים kedeshim or consecrated persons. The word implies all kinds of prostitutes, as well as abusers of themselves with mankind. <div eID="gen13253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13254" type="x-p"/> Wove hangings for the grove - For Asherah; curtains or tent coverings for the places where the rites of the impure goddess were performed. See at the end of <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.26">2Kgs 21:26</reference> (note).
entries.0df40be17faf36c2ed78b7a4ba23b8fa5b12378f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> The gate of Joshua - The place where he, as governor of the city, heard and decided causes. Near this we find there were public altars, where sometimes the true God, at other times false gods, were honored.
entries.49d53d27e5e059e9aeeabf072c2e4a6e35dfcd8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen13255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13256" type="x-p"/> The priests of the high places came not up - As these priests had offered sacrifices on the high places, though it was to the true God, yet they were not thought proper to be employed immediately about the temple; but as they were acknowledged to belong to the priesthood, they had a right to their support; therefore a portion of the tithes, offerings, and unleavened bread, shew-bread, etc., was appointed to them for their support. Thus they were treated as priests who had some infirmity which rendered it improper for them to minister at the altar. See <reference osisRef="Lev.21.17">Lev 21:17</reference>, etc., and particularly <reference osisRef="Lev.21.22">Lev 21:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.23">Lev 21:23</reference>.
entries.36c819e409c473fb371cc20c3a184c703ed7e9dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen13256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> He defiled Topheth - St. Jerome says that Topheth was a fine and pleasant place, well watered with fountains, and adorned with gardens. The valley of the son of Hinnom, or Gehenna, was in one part; here it appears the sacred rites of Molech were performed, and to this all the filth of the city was carried, and perpetual fires were kept up in order to consume it. Hence it has been considered a type of hell; and in this sense it is used in the New Testament. <div eID="gen13257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13258" type="x-p"/> It is here said that Josiah defiled this place that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire. He destroyed the image of Molech, and so polluted the place where he stood, or his temple, that it was rendered in every way abominable. The rabbins say that Topheth had its name from תף toph, a drum, because instruments of this kind were used to drown the cries of the children that were put into the burning arms of Molech, to be scorched to death. This may be as true as the following definition: "Topheth, or the valley of the son of Hinnom, was a place near Jerusalem, where the filth and offal of the city were thrown, and where a constant fire was kept up to consume the wretched remains of executed criminals. It was a human shambles, a public chopping-block, where the arms and legs of men and women were quartered off by thousands." Query, On what authority do such descriptions rest?
entries.4634596561296cd2a2d846687f4dc30de68a053e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen13258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13259" type="x-p"/> The horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun - Jarchi says that those who adored the sun had horses which they mounted every morning to go out to meet the sun at his rising. Throughout the East the horse, because of his swiftness and utility, was dedicated to the sun; and the Greeks and Romans feigned that the chariot of the sun was drawn by four horses - Pyroeis, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.11">2Kgs 2:11</reference>. <div eID="gen13259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13260" type="x-p"/> Whether these were living or sculptured horses, we cannot tell; the latter is the more reasonable supposition.
entries.3cca5a903b72baa75179b36f9d6b037f99652d21: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen13260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> On the top of the upper chamber - Altars built on the flat roof of the house. Such altars were erected to the sun, moon, stars, etc.
entries.6c43da53c48175482f363597d2aa714830b2e17a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> Mount of corruption - This, says Jarchi, following the Chaldee, was the mount of Olives, for this is the mount המשחה hammishchah, of unction; but because of the idolatrous purposes for which it was used, the Scripture changed the appellation to the mount המשחית hammashchith, of corruption. <div eID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> Ashtoreth the abomination, etc. - See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.7">1Kgs 11:7</reference> (note).
entries.2db90a44a7691cedb56d47832fb0887eeeb18394: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> Filled their places with the bones of men - This was allowed to be the utmost defilement to which any thing could be exposed.
entries.97b2255f5f90508bfd1db7c1c204a0cc2366c022: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13265" type="x-p"/> And as Josiah turned himself - This verse is much more complete in the Septuagint, and in the Hexaplar Syriac version at Paris. I shall give the whole, making a distinction where, in those versions, any thing is added: "And as Josiah turned himself, he spied the sepulchres that were there in the mount, and sent and took the bones out of the sepulchres, and burnt them upon the altar, and polluted it: according to the word of the Lord which the man of God proclaimed [when Jeroboam stood by the altar at the feast. And turning about, he cast his eyes on the sepulcher of the man of God] who proclaimed these words." See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2">1Kgs 13:2</reference> (note), where these things were predicted, and see the notes there.
entries.d95746e666517e761cd57df5bfabe6befbfb9cb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen13265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13266" type="x-p"/> What title is that - There was either a stone, an image, or an inscription here: the old prophet no doubt took care to have the place made sufficiently remarkable.
entries.f8037db17f2304bc7eddd2db0db9fc535a537b53: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13267" type="x-p"/> The prophet that came out of Samaria - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.32">1Kgs 13:32</reference>.
entries.8d479b2328464880b29bc9b44cb5d41e83a96508: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen13267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> That were in the cities of Samaria - Israel had now no king; and Josiah, of the blood royal of Judah, had certainly a direct right to the kingdom; he had, at this time, an especial commission from God, to reform every abuse through the whole land - all that ground that was given by the Lord as an inheritance to the twelve sons of Jacob. Therefore he had every right to carry his plans of reformation into the Samaritan states.
entries.0b59e7ab4c43a28f2a4bcf330272fdd94b7aab97: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> Slew all the priests - The lives of these, as corrupters of the people, were forfeited to the law.
entries.b261acf68efc77c0bfb37d9bae000702bc5cb329: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> Surely there was not holden such a passover - Not one on purer principles, more heartily joined in by the people present, more literally consecrated, or more religiously observed. The words do not apply to the number present, but to the manner and spirit. See the particulars and mode of celebrating this passover in 2 Chronicles 35:1-18 (note).
entries.396f98d55859aa1468506eb36716cc5d0b4c757e: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13271" type="x-p"/> The workers with familiar spirits - See on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.5">2Kgs 21:5</reference> (note). <div eID="gen13271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13272" type="x-p"/> And the images - The teraphim. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>.
